name: The Serac Tide

detectability.signature: Strain-gradient harmonics beneath a visible prismatic ripple in the starfield, readable at 480,000 kilometers

proximity: Hull micro-stress becomes audible as intermittent creaking
Navigational instruments jitter against one another by arcminutes
Loose objects slide in slow, directionless drifts
contact: Mooring lines and docking clamps fail under differential pull
Structural frames take visible elastic flexing
Sensor masts and antennae snap at their roots
prolonged_exposure: Accelerated metal fatigue spreading across the entire airframe
Crew injuries from shifting cargo and failing fittings

phenomena: Tidal forces audibly stressing hull structures
Visible prismatic scoring of the starfield along shear planes
Debris sorted into improbably neat density bands
Objects accelerating without thrust during surge peaks
hazards: Structural collapse from differential tidal stress
Hull breach along stress fractures during surges
Erratic surge timing defeating safety margins
opportunities: Density-sorted mineral streams ripe for salvage
Rare element concentration settling in the tide's debris bands
known_incidents: 2296 - Tug Andelfingen broke apart at surge peak; her wreck is now a marked hazard
2333 - Salvage guild lost two crawlers to a flood tide that arrived days early
description: Wrapped around the husk of a dead binary pair, the Serac Tide is a standing wave of gravitational shear visible as a slow prismatic ripple in the starfield. Space itself appears scored, as though a glacier of transparent stress were calving in silence. Approach sensors paint overlapping strain-gradients that rise and fall to the rhythm of an unseen sea.

The zone surges on a nineteen-day cycle; at flood tide hulls groan and moored structures walk their anchors, while at slack water the interior rewards careful passage. The surge timing wanders without warning, sometimes arriving days early, and it has ruined more than one salvage timetable. Metal fatigues here faster than anywhere else in the sector, and old hands claim they can date a hull's harbor history by its creaks.

Rimward miners first mapped the Tide while chasing a debris stream that had been sorted, impossibly neatly, into bands by density. The tug Andelfingen broke her keel at second flood in 2296, and her slowly tearing wreck became the sector's grimmest navigation lesson. Salvage guilds still work the zone between surges, harvesting the tidewater's tidy mineral sorting.

The binary's corpse ticks toward some final collapse, and each survey finds the surges a little stronger and a little less regular. Station Seracwatch sells flood-tide forecasts that are honest about being guesses. Travelers should treat the Tide as sailors treat a riptide: enter at slack, leave early, and never trust the calm.
